en jakke.explanation: "En jakke" means "a jacket". A thicker, longer one is "en frakke" (a coat). A useful phrase is "Tag en jakke med" (Take a jacket with you).

sentence.da: Tag din **jakke** på, det er koldt.
sentence.en: Put your jacket on, it is cold.

en julegave.explanation: "En julegave" means "a Christmas present". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "en gave" (a gift), and "at købe julegaver" means "to buy Christmas presents".

sentence.da: Under juletræet ligger en **julegave** til dig.
sentence.en: Under the Christmas tree there is a Christmas present for you.

et job.explanation: "Et job" means "a job", a particular position: "Jeg har et nyt job" means "I have a new job". "Arbejde" is the work itself: "Jeg skal på arbejde" means "I am going to work".

sentence.da: Jeg arbejder hver dag, og jeg kan lide mit **job**.
sentence.en: I work every day, and I like my job.

et jordbær.explanation: "Et jordbær" means "a strawberry". It is made of "jord" (earth, ground) and "et bær" (a berry).

sentence.da: Om sommeren spiser vi **jordbær** med fløde.
sentence.en: In the summer we eat strawberries with cream.

et juletræ.explanation: "Et juletræ" means "a Christmas tree". It is made of "jul" (Christmas) and "et træ" (a tree).

sentence.da: Til jul har vi et **juletræ** i stuen med lys på.
sentence.en: At Christmas we have a Christmas tree in the living room with lights on it.

ja.explanation: "Ja" means "yes". "Ja, tak" means "yes, please" and is the polite way to accept an offer. If a question has "ikke" (not) in it, like "Kommer du ikke?" (Aren't you coming?), Danes answer "jo" (yes) instead of "ja".

sentence.da: Vil du have kaffe? **Ja**, tak.
sentence.en: Do you want coffee? Yes, please.

januar.explanation: "Januar" means "January". Month names are written with a small letter ("januar"), while English "January" has a capital letter. You can say "midt i januar" (in the middle of January).

sentence.da: Det er koldt i **januar**.
sentence.en: It is cold in January.

japan.explanation: "Japan" means "Japan". The "J" is pronounced like an English "Y", so it sounds like "YAH-pan".

sentence.da: Sushi kommer fra **Japan**.
sentence.en: Sushi comes from Japan.

japansk.explanation: "Japansk" means "Japanese". It is written with a small letter ("japansk"), while English "Japanese" has a capital letter. On its own it is also the name of the language: "Jeg taler japansk" (I speak Japanese).

sentence.da: Sushi er **japansk** mad.
sentence.en: Sushi is Japanese food.

jeg.explanation: "Jeg" means "I" and is written with a capital letter only at the start of a sentence, as in "Du og jeg" (you and I). It sounds roughly like "yai". When it is "me" instead, the word is "mig", as in "Han ser mig" (He sees me).

sentence.da: **Jeg** bor i København.
sentence.en: I live in Copenhagen.

jeg er enig.explanation: "Jeg er enig" means "I agree". Danish literally says "I am agreed" instead of using a word like "agree". To say who you agree with, add "med" (with): "Jeg er enig med dig" (I agree with you).

sentence.da: **Jeg er enig** med dig.
sentence.en: I agree with you.

jeg er ked af det.explanation: "Jeg er ked af det" means "I'm sad", and also "I'm sorry" when you regret something. For a quick apology like bumping into someone, "undskyld" (sorry, excuse me) is more common; "jeg er ked af det" sounds more heartfelt.

sentence.da: **Jeg er ked af det**, men jeg kan ikke komme i dag.
sentence.en: I'm sorry, but I can't come today.

jeg forstår ikke.explanation: "Jeg forstår ikke" means "I don't understand". "Forstår" means "understand" and "ikke" means "not". To say "I don't understand it", put "det" (it) before "ikke": "Jeg forstår det ikke". To ask for help, add "kan du gentage det?" (can you repeat that?).

sentence.da: Du taler for hurtigt, **jeg forstår ikke**.
sentence.en: You speak too fast, I don't understand.

jeg har det godt.explanation: "Jeg har det godt" means "I'm doing well" and is the usual answer to "hvordan har du det?" (how are you?). Danish literally says "I have it good", so you need "det" (it); "jeg er godt" would sound wrong. For much the same idea you can say "det går godt" (it's going well).

sentence.da: Tak, **jeg har det godt**. Og dig?
sentence.en: Thanks, I'm doing well. And you?

jeg har det skidt.explanation: "Jeg har det skidt" means "I'm not doing well" and works for feeling ill as well as feeling down. "Skidt" means "badly". A milder way to say it is "jeg har det ikke så godt" (I'm not doing so well).

sentence.da: **Jeg har det skidt**, for jeg er syg.
sentence.en: I'm not doing well, because I'm sick.

forms.da: Hvad hedder du? Jeg hedder Lars.

jeg hedder….explanation: "Jeg hedder…" means "my name is…" and you add your name after it. It literally means "I am called…", from "at hedde" (to be called). A common reply is "Dejligt at møde dig" (Nice to meet you).

sentence.da: **Jeg hedder** Anna, og du?
sentence.en: My name is Anna, and you?

jeg kommer fra….explanation: "Jeg kommer fra…" means "I'm from…" and you add a country or town after it. It literally means "I come from…". It answers "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where are you from?). For where you live now, say "jeg bor i…" (I live in…).

sentence.da: **Jeg kommer fra** Canada.
sentence.en: I'm from Canada.

forms.da: Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe.
Jeg vil gerne have to billetter.

jeg vil gerne have.explanation: "Jeg vil gerne have" means "I would like" and is the polite way to order or ask for something. Put the thing you want after "have". "Gerne" (gladly) makes it sound friendly; "jeg vil have" without it is blunt, like "I want".

sentence.da: **Jeg vil gerne have** en kop te.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of tea.

jer.explanation: "Jer" means "you" when you talk to more than one person, as in "Jeg kan se jer" (I can see you all). It is also used after words like "til" (to) and "med" (with). When you say what the group does, the word is "I", as in "I er søde" (you all are nice). For one person the word is "dig".

sentence.da: Børn, jeg har en gave til **jer**.
sentence.en: Children, I have a gift for you all.

jeres.explanation: "Jeres" means "your" or "yours" when you talk to more than one person, as in "jeres hus" (your house). It stays the same before any word. For one person you use "din", "dit" or "dine" (your).

sentence.da: Mor og far, er det **jeres** bil?
sentence.en: Mum and Dad, is that your car?

jo.explanation: "Jo" has two uses. It means "yes" when you answer a question that has "ikke" (not) in it: "Kommer du ikke?" (Aren't you coming?) "Jo!" (Yes, I am!). Inside a sentence it adds a feeling of "you know" or "of course", as in "det er jo rigtigt" (it is, you know, right). For ordinary yes answers use "ja" (yes).

sentence.da: Kan du ikke lide kaffe? **Jo**, det kan jeg.
sentence.en: Don't you like coffee? Yes, I do.

jord.explanation: "Jord" means "earth" or "soil": the soil that plants grow in, and also the ground you stand on. With a capital letter, "Jorden" is the planet Earth. For the floor inside a house Danes say "gulv" (floor), not "jord".

sentence.da: Planter har brug for vand og **jord**.
sentence.en: Plants need water and soil.

juice.explanation: "Juice" means "juice". To say what kind, put the fruit in front, as in "appelsinjuice" (orange juice) or "æblejuice" (apple juice).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker et glas **juice** til morgenmad.
sentence.en: I drink a glass of juice for breakfast.

jul.explanation: "Jul" means "Christmas". You say "til jul" (at Christmas) and "i julen" (during the Christmas season), usually with no word for "a" in front. The greeting is "Glædelig jul!" (Merry Christmas!).

sentence.da: Vi har et juletræ og får gaver til **jul**.
sentence.en: We have a Christmas tree and get presents at Christmas.

juleaften.explanation: "Juleaften" means "Christmas Eve", the evening of 24 December. You normally use it with no "en" (a) in front, as in "på juleaften" (on Christmas Eve).

sentence.da: På **juleaften** pynter vi juletræet og får gaver.
sentence.en: On Christmas Eve we decorate the Christmas tree and get presents.

juli.explanation: "Juli" means "July" and is written with a small letter ("juli"), while English "July" has a capital letter. It looks close to "juni" (June), so check the middle: "juli" has an l and "juni" has an n.

sentence.da: Mange danskere har ferie i **juli**.
sentence.en: Many Danes are on vacation in July.

juni.explanation: "Juni" means "June" and is written with a small letter ("juni"), while English "June" has a capital letter. It looks close to "juli" (July), so check the middle: "juni" has an n and "juli" has an l.

sentence.da: Det er lyst længe i **juni**.
sentence.en: It stays light for a long time in June.
